d.title: Two embedding methods, because the two jobs are not the same
d.caption: `embed_documents` takes a list and returns one vector each; `embed_query` takes one string and returns one vector. **The split looks redundant and is not** — several embedding models are trained asymmetrically, with a different instruction prefix for a document than for a query, and the two methods are where that difference lives. Implement only one and you get a retriever that works and quietly under-performs, which is the hardest class of bug in this course.

d.title: A retriever is a Runnable, so it pipes
d.caption: `invoke('revenue')` returns documents and `isinstance(r, Runnable)` is `True` — and those two facts together are why 5.7 can write an entire RAG pipeline as **one LCEL expression** rather than as a function that calls a retriever and then calls a model. The uniformity from 1.1 doing the work again: nothing about retrieval needed special support in the composition layer, because retrieval satisfied the one method the composition layer knows about.

nodes.label: So it pipes into a chain
And retrieval needed no special support

d.title: The description is prompt, not documentation
d.caption: The name, the description **and** the argument schema are all sent to the model. Which makes the description **prompt rather than documentation** — and 3.1 is entirely about that distinction, because **it decides whether the tool gets called at all**. It is the single most common reason an agent ignores a tool that would have answered the question: the implementation was fine, the schema was fine, and the one sentence describing it did not separate it from its neighbours.

nodes.label: The commonest cause of an ignored tool

d.title: Three chain starts, three chain ends — the tree is observable
d.caption: A callback handler sees every start and end in the chain, not just the outer one: a three-step chain fires **three starts and three ends**, nested. That symmetry is the useful invariant — **starts without matching ends mean something raised inside a step** — and it is the mechanism every tracing backend in this course is built on. 10.4's span tree in the GenAI course is the same idea with a wire protocol attached.

d.title: Five components, one pipeline, and Document is the type that joins them
d.caption: The pieces connect through a single carrier: **`Document(page_content, metadata)`**. A loader produces them; a splitter produces more of them with the **same metadata and smaller content**; embeddings turn the content into vectors; the store holds the pair; and a retriever hands the Documents back. Which is why metadata filtering works at all — the metadata survives every stage untouched, so a filter written at retrieval time can reference a field the loader set.

nodes.label: So metadata survives end to end

d.title: A function is already enough, until it needs to carry something
d.caption: For a stateless transformation a plain function is a complete component — `RunnableLambda` wraps one explicitly and the pipe will coerce a bare function for you, producing something with all four of `invoke`, `batch`, `stream` and `ainvoke`. **Reach for a subclass only when you need something a function cannot carry**: configuration, validation, or a meaningful name in a trace. The last is the practical one: a `RunnableLambda` wrapping a lambda shows up in a span tree as `RunnableLambda`, **which is unhelpful at three in the morning.**

nodes.label: Or a name in the trace

d.title: Implement the one required method and the protocol arrives
d.caption: The same pattern as the chat model in 1.2: define `_call` (or `invoke`) and `batch`, `stream` and the async half are **inherited, not written.** That consistency is the point, and it gives you a question to ask of any base class in this library: **which single method is it defined in terms of?** Answer that and you know both what you have to write and what you get for free.

nodes.label: So ask of any base class
nodes.sub: which one method is it defined on?

d.title: Writing your own parser is where 1.4's rule becomes literally true
d.caption: The parser handles clean input and prose around it, and **raises on commas** — deliberately, because a list parser that silently splits on the wrong delimiter is 1.4's exact failure. The part worth copying is that `get_format_instructions` is **implemented in the same class**: 1.4's rule was that a parser and its instructions must travel together, and writing your own is where you can make that literally true rather than a convention someone has to remember.

d.title: Six components, three of them yours, one expression
d.caption: A prompt, a model, a built-in parser, a custom parser, a coerced function and a custom Runnable — **three written for this chain and three from the library** — compose in a single `|` expression and inspect as a flat list of six steps. Which is the chapter's claim discharged: the protocol did not care which half of the chain you wrote, and nothing in the composition needed to know that `BulletListParser` was not shipped with the package.

d.title: The chain ran and the answer is wrong
d.caption: A component received a list where it expected a string, did something defensible with it, and the chain completed. **Nothing raised** — which is the failure this whole lesson has been circling. Adding an explicit type check turns it into `TypeError: TruncateWords expected str, got list` at the point of the mistake. Worth doing on **any component whose expected input is not obvious from its position**, which is most custom components: a reader cannot tell from `| TruncateWords(n=2)` what the previous step produced.

nodes.label: A list arrives where a str was expected
'| TruncateWords(n=2)'
nodes.sub: tells a reader nothing about its input

d.title: The dependency, stated rather than defended
d.caption: **29 packages in `langchain-core`'s install closure and 34 in `langgraph`'s.** That is the honest cost line and it is worth leading with: not a large dependency by modern Python standards, and not free — **29 packages is 29 things with release cadences, CVE feeds and transitive pins**, and "we added a framework" is a sentence that gets asked about in a review. Quoting the number is a better answer than arguing that it is small.

d.title: On a single call, the uniformity is paid for and not used
d.caption: Both versions of a one-shot question-and-answer are about the same size, and **the raw SDK version is clearer to someone who has not used LangChain** — which on most teams is most people. The reason is not that the framework is heavy here; it is that **there is no composition being exploited.** One call has nothing to compose with, so the uniformity that 1.1 argued for is a cost with no corresponding benefit on this task.

nodes.label: So the uniformity is paid for, unused

d.title: Three costs a line count cannot show
d.caption: A line-count comparison is the argument everyone reaches for and it measures the least important axis. **The abstraction your team has to learn** before they can read the chain at all is the largest of the three on most teams. **A dependency whose release cadence you now track** brings breaking changes you did not schedule. And **indirection in the traceback** — a failure inside a step inside a sequence — is the one that is invisible until the first production incident.

items.label: The abstraction to learn
items.sub: paid once per person, by most of the team

items.label: A cadence you now track
items.sub: breaking changes you did not schedule

items.label: Traceback indirection
items.sub: invisible until the first production incident

d.title: The test, and what to do when it comes out ambiguous
d.caption: The decision rule is a count rather than a judgement, which is what makes it usable. **None yes: use the SDK**, because you are paying for uniformity you will not use. **Two or more yes: use the framework**, because each of those features is cheap with uniform components and expensive without. And the middle row is the honest one — **exactly one yes is a judgement call**, and the suggestion is concrete: write the raw version plus the one feature, and revisit at the second.
